==Problem==
For certain real numbers <imath>a</imath>, <imath>b</imath>, and <imath>c</imath>, the polynomial <cmath>g(x) = x^3 + ax^2 + x + 10</cmath>has three distinct roots, and each root of <imath>g(x)</imath> is also a root of the polynomial <cmath>f(x) = x^4 + x^3 + bx^2 + 100x + c.</cmath>What is <imath>f(1)</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ -9009 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\ -8008 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\ -7007 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\ -6006 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\ -5005</imath>

==Solution 1==
<imath>f(x)</imath> must have four roots, three of which are roots of <imath>g(x)</imath>. Using the fact that every polynomial has a unique factorization into its roots, and since the leading coefficient of <imath>f(x)</imath> and <imath>g(x)</imath> are the same, we know that

<cmath>f(x)=g(x)(x+p)</cmath>

where <imath>-p\in\mathbb{R}</imath> is the fourth root of <imath>f(x)</imath>. 
(Using <imath>(x+p) = (x-r))</imath> instead of <imath>(x-r)</imath> makes the following computations less messy.)
Substituting <imath>g(x)</imath> and expanding, we find that

<cmath>\begin{align*}f(x)&=(x^3+ax^2+x+10)(x+p)\\
&=x^4+(a+p)x^3+(1+ap)x^2+(10+p)x+10p.\end{align*}</cmath>

Comparing coefficients with <imath>f(x)</imath>, we see that

<cmath>\begin{align*}
a+p&=1\\
1+ap=b\\
10+p&=100\\
10p&=c.\\
\end{align*}</cmath>


Let's solve for <imath>a,b,c,</imath> and <imath>p</imath>. Since <imath>10+p=100</imath>, <imath>p=90</imath>.

Since <imath>a+p=1</imath>, <imath>a=-89</imath>. 

(Solution 1.1 branches from here and takes a shortcut.)

<imath>c=(10)(90)=900</imath>.

Then, since <imath>b=1+ap</imath>, <imath>b=-8009</imath>. Thus,

<cmath>f(x)=x^4+x^3-8009x^2+100x+900.</cmath>

(Solution 1.2 branches from here and takes another shortcut)

Taking <imath>f(1)</imath>, we find that

<cmath>\begin{align*}
f(1)&=1^4+1^3-8009(1)^2+100(1)+900\\
&=1+1-8009+100+900\\
&=\boxed{\bold{(C)}\, -7007}.\\
\end{align*}</cmath>

===Solution 1.1===
A faster ending to Solution 1 is as follows.

<cmath>\begin{align*}
f(1)&=(1+p)(1^3+a\cdot1^2+1+10)\\
&=(91)(-77)\\
&= (7)(13)(11)(-7) = (1001)(-7) \\
&=\boxed{\bold{(C)}\, -7007}.\\
\end{align*}</cmath>

===Solution 1.2===
Also a faster ending to Solution 1 is as follows.

To find <imath>f(1)</imath> we just need to find the sum of the coefficients which is <imath>1 + 1 - 8009 + 100 + 900= \boxed{\bold{(C)} \ , -7007}.</imath>

==Solution 2==
We notice that the constant term of <imath>f(x)=c</imath> and the constant term in <imath>g(x)=10</imath>. Because <imath>f(x)</imath> can be factored as <imath>g(x) \cdot (x- r)</imath> (where <imath>r</imath> is the unshared root of <imath>f(x)</imath>, we see that using the constant term, <imath>-10 \cdot r = c</imath> and therefore <imath>r = -\frac{c}{10}</imath>.
Now we once again write <imath>f(x)</imath> out in factored form: 

<cmath>f(x) = g(x)\cdot (x-r) = (x^3+ax^2+x+10)(x+\frac{c}{10})</cmath>.

We can expand the expression on the right-hand side to get:

<cmath>f(x) = x^4+(a+\frac{c}{10})x^3+(1+\frac{ac}{10})x^2+(10+\frac{c}{10})x+c</cmath>

Now we have <imath>f(x) = x^4+(a+\frac{c}{10})x^3+(1+\frac{ac}{10})x^2+(10+\frac{c}{10})x+c=x^4+x^3+bx^2+100x+c</imath>.

Simply looking at the coefficients for each corresponding term (knowing that they must be equal), we have the equations:
<cmath>10+\frac{c}{10}=100 \Rightarrow c=900</cmath>
<cmath>a+\frac{c}{10} = 1, c=900 \Rightarrow a + 90 =1 \Rightarrow a= -89</cmath>

and finally,

<cmath>1+\frac{ac}{10} = b = 1+\frac{-89 \cdot 900}{10} = b = -8009</cmath>.

We know that <imath>f(1)</imath> is the sum of its coefficients, hence <imath>1+1+b+100+c</imath>. We substitute the values we obtained for <imath>b</imath> and <imath>c</imath> into this expression to get <imath>f(1) = 1 + 1 + (-8009) + 100 + 900 = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\,-7007}</imath>.

==Solution 3==

Let <imath>r_1,r_2,</imath> and <imath>r_3</imath> be the roots of <imath>g(x)</imath>. Let <imath>r_4</imath> be the additional root of <imath>f(x)</imath>. Then from Vieta's formulas on the quadratic term of <imath>g(x)</imath> and the cubic term of <imath>f(x)</imath>, we obtain the following:

<cmath>\begin{align*}
r_1+r_2+r_3&=-a \\ 
r_1+r_2+r_3+r_4&=-1
\end{align*}</cmath>

Thus <imath>r_4=a-1</imath>.

Now applying Vieta's formulas on the constant term of <imath>g(x)</imath>, the linear term of <imath>g(x)</imath>, and the linear term of <imath>f(x)</imath>, we obtain:

<cmath>\begin{align*}
r_1r_2r_3  & = -10\\
r_1r_2+r_2r_3+r_3r_1 &= 1\\ 
r_1r_2r_3+r_2r_3r_4+r_3r_4r_1+r_4r_1r_2  & = -100\\
\end{align*}</cmath>

Substituting for <imath>r_1r_2r_3</imath> in the bottom equation and factoring the remainder of the expression, we obtain:

<cmath>-10+(r_1r_2+r_2r_3+r_3r_1)r_4=-10+r_4=-100</cmath>

It follows that <imath>r_4=-90</imath>. But <imath>r_4=a-1</imath> so <imath>a=-89</imath>

Now we can factor <imath>f(x)</imath> in terms of <imath>g(x)</imath> as

<cmath>f(x)=(x-r_4)g(x)=(x+90)g(x)</cmath>

Then <imath>f(1)=91g(1)</imath> and

<cmath>g(1)=1^3-89\cdot 1^2+1+10=-77</cmath>

Hence <imath>f(1)=91\cdot(-77)=\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\,-7007}</imath>.

==Solution 4 (Risky)==
Let the roots of <imath>g(x)</imath> be <imath>r_1</imath>, <imath>r_2</imath>, and <imath>r_3</imath>. Let the roots of <imath>f(x)</imath> be <imath>r_1</imath>, <imath>r_2</imath>, <imath>r_3</imath>, and <imath>r_4</imath>. From Vieta's, we have:
<cmath>\begin{align*}
r_1+r_2+r_3=-a \\
r_1+r_2+r_3+r_4=-1 \\
r_4=a-1
\end{align*}</cmath>
The fourth root is <imath>a-1</imath>. Since <imath>r_1</imath>, <imath>r_2</imath>, and <imath>r_3</imath> are common roots, we have:
<cmath>\begin{align*}
f(x)=g(x)(x-(a-1)) \\
f(1)=g(1)(1-(a-1)) \\
f(1)=(a+12)(2-a) \\
f(1)=-(a+12)(a-2) \\
\end{align*}</cmath>
Let <imath>a-2=k</imath>:
<cmath>\begin{align*}
f(1)=-k(k+14)
\end{align*}</cmath>
Note that <imath>-7007=-1001\cdot(7)=-(7\cdot(11)\cdot(13))\cdot(7)=-91\cdot(77)</imath>
This gives us a pretty good guess of <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\, -7007}</imath>.

==Solution 5==
First off, let's get rid of the <imath>x^4</imath> term by finding <imath>h(x)=f(x)-xg(x)</imath>. This polynomial consists of the difference of two polynomials with <imath>3</imath> common factors, so it must also have these factors. The polynomial is <imath>h(x)=(1-a)x^3 + (b-1)x^2 + 90x + c</imath>, and must be equal to <imath>(1-a)g(x)</imath>. Equating the coefficients, we get <imath>3</imath> equations. We will tackle the situation one equation at a time, starting the <imath>x</imath> terms. Looking at the coefficients, we get <imath>\dfrac{90}{1-a} = 1</imath>. <cmath>\therefore 90=1-a.</cmath> The solution to the previous is obviously <imath>a=-89</imath>. We can now find <imath>b</imath> and <imath>c</imath>. <imath>\dfrac{b-1}{1-a} = a</imath>, <cmath>\therefore b-1=a(1-a)=-89*90=-8010</cmath> and <imath>b=-8009</imath>. Finally <imath>\dfrac{c}{1-a} = 10</imath>, <cmath>\therefore c=10(1-a)=10*90=900</cmath> Solving the original problem, <imath>f(1)=1 + 1 + b + 100 + c = 102+b+c=102+900-8009=\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\, -7007}</imath>.

==Solution 6==
Simple polynomial division is a feasible method. Even though we have variables, we can equate terms at the end of the division so that we can cancel terms. Doing the division of <imath>\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}</imath> eventually brings us the final step <imath>(1-a)x^3 + (b-1)x^2 + 90x + c</imath> minus <imath>(1-a)x^3 - (a-a^2)x^2 + (1-a)x + 10(1-a)</imath> after we multiply <imath>f(x)</imath> by <imath>(1-a)</imath>. Now we equate coefficients of same-degree <imath>x</imath> terms. This gives us <imath> 10(1-a) = c, b-1 = a - a^2, 1-a = 90 \Rightarrow a = -89, c = 900, b = -8009</imath>. We are interested in finding <imath>f(1)</imath>, which equals <imath>1^4 + 1^3 -8009\cdot1^2 + 100\cdot1 + 900 = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\,-7007}</imath>. ~skyscraper

==Solution 7==
We first note that <imath>f(x) = g(x) \cdot q(x) + r(x)</imath> where <imath>q</imath> is the quotient function and <imath>r</imath> is the remainder function.

Clearly, <imath>r(x) = 0</imath> because every single root in <imath>g</imath> is also in <imath>f</imath>, thus implying <imath>g</imath> divides <imath>f</imath>.
So, we wish to find <imath>f(1) = g(1) \cdot q(1)</imath>.

Such an expression for <imath>g(1)</imath> is pretty clean here as we can obtain <imath>g(1) = a + 12</imath>, so we rewrite <imath>f(1) = (a + 12) \cdot q(1)</imath>.
Well, now we need to know how <imath>q</imath> is expressed in order to obtain <imath>q(1)</imath>. This motivates us to long divide to obtain the quotient function. After simple long division <imath>q(x) = x + (1 - a)</imath>. In addition, what is left over, namely <imath>r(x)</imath>, has a constant piece of <imath>a + 89</imath> (you'll see in a few sentences why we only care about particularly the constant piece).

Now we can write: <imath>f(1) = (a + 12) \cdot (2 - a)</imath>.

Now, as we have already established <imath>r(x) = 0</imath> for ALL <imath>x</imath> that means <imath>r(0)</imath> or the constant piece is <imath>0</imath>, so <imath>89 + a = 0</imath>, in which we obtain <imath>a = -89</imath>. We now plug this back into our equation for <imath>f(1)</imath> to get <imath>(-89 + 12)(2 - (89)) = -77 \cdot 91 = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\,-7007}</imath>. ~triggod

==Solution 8==

Since <imath>\text{deg(f(x))}=\text{deg(g(x))}+1</imath>, we can write<cmath>(f(x)=g(x)\left(x-r \right) \Longrightarrow \left(x^3+ax^2+x+10 \right) \left(x-r \right)=x^4+x^3+bx^2+100x+c.</cmath>Expanding this we get<cmath>x^4+\left(a-r \right)x^3+\left(1-ar \right)x^2+\left(10-r \right)x-10r=x^4+x^3+bx^2+100+c.</cmath>From coefficient matching we get the following equations:<cmath>a-r=1</cmath><cmath>1-ar=b</cmath><cmath>10-r=100</cmath><cmath>c=-10r.</cmath>Obviously, the third equation results in <imath>r</imath> being <imath>=90</imath>, and plugging that into the fourth equation we get <imath>c=900</imath>. Now, we can also plug in <imath>r=-90</imath> to the first equation to get <imath>a=-89</imath>. Finally, plugging <imath>a</imath> and <imath>r</imath> into the second equation we find that <imath>b=-8009</imath>. We are asked to find <imath>f(1)</imath> which is simply <imath>b+c+102 = 7007 \Longrightarrow \boxed{C}</imath>.

-jb2015007

==Solution 9 (Vieta System)==
Let <imath>p,q,</imath> and <imath>r</imath> be the roots of <imath>g(x),</imath> and <imath>s</imath> be the additional root of <imath>f(x).</imath> By Vieta's formulas, it follows that
<cmath>\begin{cases}p+q+r=-a &(1)\\pq+pr+qr=1 &(2)\\pqr=-10 &(3)\\ p+q+r+s=-1 &(4)\\ pqrs=c &(5)\\pq+pr+ps+qr+qs+rs=b &(6)\\
pqr+pqs+prs+qrs=-100 &(7)\end{cases}</cmath>
Looking at <imath>(7),</imath> we have that
<cmath>pqr+s(pq+pr+qr)=-10+s=-100\implies s=-90</cmath>
then looking at <imath>(5)</imath> we have that 
<cmath>c=-10\cdot-90=900</cmath>
looking at <imath>(4)</imath> yields
<cmath>-1-s=-a\implies a=s+1=-89</cmath>
and looking at <imath>(6)</imath> yields
<cmath>1+s(p+q+r)=1-as=1-90\cdot89=-8009=b.</cmath>
Thus,
<cmath>f(1)=1+1-8009+100+900=\boxed{\textbf{(C) }-7007}</cmath>
~shockfront99

==General Notes==
<imath>f(1)</imath> for any polynomial is simply the sum of the coefficients of the polynomial.

<imath>f(x)/g(x) = x+r</imath> must have real <imath>r</imath>. Both <imath>f</imath> and <imath>g</imath> have all real coefficients, and so odd-degree <imath>g</imath> must have an odd number of real roots, and even-degree <imath>f</imath> must have an even number of real roots, so <imath>f</imath>'s single additional root must be real.


<imath>77 * 91 = 7 * 11 * 7 * 13</imath>, and <imath>7*11*13=1001</imath> is a good number sense fact to know. It's interesting because <imath>1001= 10^3+1</imath> and the 3 nearest primes to <imath> 10 </imath> are <imath>7,11,13</imath>.
